terms.def: The IEEE standard family for wireless LANs. It defines the MAC and PHY layers, management frames, and the a, b, g, n, ac and ax amendments.
The IEEE standard for VLAN tagging. The tag is 4 bytes: a 16-bit TPID and a 16-bit TCI holding PCP, DEI and the 12-bit VID.
The VLAN tagging standard: a 4-byte tag with a TPID of 0x8100, 3 bits of priority, 1 bit of drop eligibility and a 12-bit VLAN ID.
Authentication, Authorization and Accounting. Identity, permission and audit trail, configured with aaa new-model and method lists.
Authentication, Authorization and Accounting. The framework behind enterprise wireless identity, normally implemented with RADIUS.
Area Border Router — the router joining an OSPF area to the backbone, and the place where area range summarization is configured.
Area Border Router — interfaces in two or more areas with at least one in Area 0. Originates Type 3 summaries and does NSSA Type 7 to Type 5 translation.

An Area Border Router (ABR) has interfaces in more than one OSPF Area (at least one must be Area 0). It keeps a separate Link State Database/SPF tree per area and advertises inter-area summary (Type-3) LSAs between areas.
An ordered set of permit and deny rules applied to traffic. Cisco ACLs end with an implicit deny, so anything not explicitly permitted is dropped.
Used to classify traffic for NAT.
A switch port belonging to one access VLAN, normally carrying untagged endpoint traffic. Configured with switchport mode access.
A port in a single VLAN carrying untagged frames to an end device — the port type PortFast and BPDU Guard are designed for.
An access control list, a set of match conditions and actions applied to traffic, typically as a filter on an interface.
Access Control List. Ordered permit and deny rules evaluated top down with first match winning and an implicit deny at the end.
Access Control List. Used for group boundaries, multicast scoping and RPF policy.
Access Control List. A match tool for IP addresses and ports, used by class maps and policy routing.

An ACL (Access Control List) is an ordered list of permit/deny rules applied to traffic (or routes, or NAT, or QoS classification...). Matching is first-match-wins top-down with an implicit deny at the end — the two rules that drive every ACL question. Classic form: standard (source only, 1–99)...
The 0–255 local ranking of how trustworthy a routing source is. Lower is better: connected 0, static 1, eBGP 20, EIGRP 90, OSPF 110, RIP 120, iBGP 200.
The 0–255 trust ranking between route sources. OSPF sits at 110, between EIGRP at 90 and RIP at 120.
The 0–255 trust ranking between route sources. EIGRP internal is 90 and external is 170 — and AD plays no part in the feasibility condition.
The trust ranking between route sources. BGP splits it sharply — eBGP 20, iBGP 200 — and a confederation peer counts as internal at 200.
The preference between route sources. Lower AD wins before metric comparison. EIGRP internal 90, OSPF 110, EIGRP external 170, eBGP 20, iBGP 200.
The application of analytics and machine learning to IT operations, including baselining, anomaly detection, event correlation and root-cause suggestions.

Ansible is a push-based, agentless automation tool: YAML playbooks declare what to do, and modules execute it against inventory hosts over SSH (no agent to install!). For networking: ios_command / ios_config modules, or RESTCONF via uri. A control node runs them; devices just need SSH.
An addressing model where one address is assigned to many devices and the network delivers to the nearest of them.
An addressing model where one address is assigned to many devices and the network delivers to the nearest of them. IPv6 made it a first-class concept.
One address configured on multiple routers. Anycast RP uses a shared loopback plus MSDP for redundancy.
Automatic Private IP Addressing: the self-assigned 169.254.0.0/16 address a DHCP client takes when no server answers. A diagnostic, not a configuration.
An EEM policy made of an event detector, an optional condition and one or more actions.
Address Resolution Protocol — maps an IPv4 address to a MAC address on the local Layer 2 segment. The IPv6 equivalent is NDP, carried over ICMPv6.
Address Resolution Protocol — maps an IPv4 address to a MAC address on the local Layer 2 segment. The IPv6 equivalent is NDP over ICMPv6.
Address Resolution Protocol — maps an IPv4 address to a MAC address on the local segment. The IPv6 equivalent is neighbour discovery.
The well-known mandatory attribute listing every AS the route traversed. It is both the loop prevention and step 3 of best path, where shorter wins.
Autonomous System Boundary Router — the OSPF router injecting external routes, and the place where summary-address is configured.
Autonomous System Boundary Router — redistributes routes from outside OSPF and originates Type 5 externals, or Type 7 inside an NSSA.
The electrical-layer handshake where two Ethernet devices agree on the highest common speed and duplex at link-up.
The maximum theoretical capacity of a link, usually expressed in bits per second. It is not the same as achieved throughput.
The path-vector routing protocol of the Internet, exchanging prefixes with path attributes between autonomous systems so operators can apply policy.
Border Gateway Protocol — the path vector protocol that routes between autonomous systems using the AS path and policy, AD 20 eBGP and 200 iBGP.
Border Gateway Protocol — the policy-driven routing protocol of the internet. Session over TCP 179, one best path per prefix, decided by a strict priority list rather than by speed.
Path-vector policy protocol; uses network/redistribute to inject routes, with origin ? on redistribute and MED often defaulting to 0.
Path-vector routing protocol whose sessions can be protected with TCP MD5 or TTL security.
Border Gateway Protocol. The path-vector protocol used to scale routing across many VPN sites.
The path-vector protocol behind MBGP, where SAFI 2 carries multicast reachability.
Border Gateway Protocol. The routing protocol extended by MP-BGP to carry VPN and multicast address families.
Border Gateway Protocol. The routing protocol used for CE to PE connectivity and for EVPN control planes and larger WAN designs.

BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the path-vector routing protocol of the Internet: it exchanges prefixes with path attributes between autonomous systems (ASes) and lets operators implement rich policy on who advertises what to whom.
BGP summarisation — combining more specific prefixes into one shorter prefix before advertising, optionally withdrawing the specifics with summary-only.
Summarising more specifics into one prefix before advertising. summary-only suppresses the details, as-set records the origins, and attributes are lost.
The deterministic best-path algorithm: Weight, Local Preference, AS_PATH, Origin, MED, eBGP over IGP metric, then router ID. The first step that differs decides.
Bridge Protocol Data Unit — the control-plane message carrying the root identity, path cost, sender identity, port identity and message age. Configuration and TCN in 802.1D.
Suppresses BPDUs on a port instead of reacting to them. It removes spanning-tree protection, so it is used rarely and deliberately.
An edge-port protection that disables a port when a BPDU is received on it, catching an unauthorised switch being connected.
Protects edge ports: when any BPDU arrives on a protected port it is placed into err-disabled. Manual or errdisable recovery to restore it.
DSL, cable or fiber internet access, typically shared, asymmetric and best effort, often using PPPoE and suitable for backup or SD-WAN transport.
The set of devices that receive a broadcast frame; limited by routers and VLAN boundaries.
The set of Layer 2 devices and interfaces that receive a Layer 2 broadcast. Routers stop broadcasts, switches forward them inside a VLAN.
The set of Layer 2 devices and interfaces that receive a Layer 2 broadcast. Routers and VLAN boundaries stop it.
The set of devices that receive a Layer 2 broadcast. A VLAN is exactly one broadcast domain, and a router is where one domain ends.
The set of devices that receive a broadcast from each other. Layer 2 loops turn one into a storm, which is what spanning tree exists to prevent.
Basic Service Set Identifier. The 48-bit MAC address of one AP radio, which identifies a specific BSS.
A shared single transmission medium where every frame reaches every node — one collision domain and one broadcast domain, with a single break taking the whole segment down.
The hardware Layer 2 forwarding database of a switch. It maps MAC address plus VLAN to egress port, and is searched by content in a single clock cycle.
The content-addressable memory holding the MAC address table, which maps a MAC address and a VLAN to a port and a VLAN to a port.
The switch’s MAC address table. Topology changes shorten its aging so stale entries do not survive a reconvergence.
Control And Provisioning of Wireless Access Points. The AP to WLC protocol, using UDP 5246 for control and UDP 5247 for data.
Cisco's intent-based campus management and assurance platform, formerly DNA Center. It provides design, policy, provisioning, automation and AI-assisted assurance.
The current name for Cisco's SD-WAN management plane, formerly vManage. It provides templates, onboarding, monitoring and REST APIs, but does not run OMP or forward user traffic.
Class-Based Weighted Fair Queuing. Egress scheduling that gives each class a guaranteed bandwidth share.
Cisco Express Forwarding — the forwarding architecture that derives a FIB and an adjacency table from the RIB so packets are forwarded in hardware.
Cisco Express Forwarding — the default forwarding architecture, the FIB plus adjacency information, with hash-based load sharing.
Cisco Express Forwarding. The IP forwarding path that feeds FECs and performs the ingress push decision.
The RF sub-bands APs transmit on. In 2.4 GHz the non-overlapping set is 1, 6 and 11; 5 GHz adds many channels including DFS.
Classless Inter-Domain Routing — writing any address as IP/prefix-length so the mask is explicit, decoupling the network boundary from the class and enabling VLSM and summarisation.
Classless Inter-Domain Routing — addressing by prefix length rather than class, which is what makes summarization possible.

Cisco IOS (Internetwork Operating System) is the classic network OS: a monolithic control-plane image with the CLI as its face. The CLI runs two families — exec (show, ping, config mode entry) and configure (global/interface/line submodes) — plus built-in help, tab completion, and ?. The...

Licensing gates feature entitlements on IOS XE: which technology packages a device may run. The legacy model used PAK keys + product activation keys / license files (EULA-based, per-box, manual); the modern model is Smart Licensing with usage reporting to a central portal. Packages on platforms:...
The number of clients and the aggregate throughput required in a given area. High density is a capacity design problem, not simply a coverage problem.
A model where centralized servers provide services and clients request them.
The connectivity path from an enterprise network into a public cloud, such as an Internet VPN, private circuit, colocation interconnect or SD-WAN overlay.
Two-tier design: distribution and core are merged into one layer above access. Fewer devices and lower cost, for small and mid-size sites.
The set of devices whose frames can collide; a switch gives one per port.
A Layer 2 segment whose devices can collide by transmitting simultaneously on a shared half-duplex medium. Switches split collision domains, hubs merge them.
Optional transitive tags in ASN:value form that let a remote peer apply policy. They never leave the router unless send-community is configured.
A debug limited by a condition, interface or ACL so the device emits output only for the traffic under investigation, reducing CPU and log impact.
An AS split into sub-ASes with eBGP-like sessions that still present one AS to the world. Confederation peers use AD 200 and attributes survive the boundaries.

Configuration backup protects the config by copying it to external storage (TFTP/FTP/SCP/USB — or a central repo like RANCID/Git) and via the IOS archive feature: archive log config keeps a numbered rollback point of config changes (show archive, configure replace) — instant diff-and-revert...
The physical termination of the medium: RJ45 for copper, LC/SC for fiber, MPO/MTP for parallel optics.

Containers package an app + its dependencies to run as isolated but kernel-shared workloads: no guest OS, no hypervisor layer — the host kernel is shared and namespaces/cgroups provide isolation and resource limits. They boot in seconds, are portable, and scale horizontally. The trade: weaker...
The logic that decides how to forward — routing protocols, ARP/ND, STP; builds the RIB and FIB.
The slow path brain of a device: it runs routing protocols, spanning tree and ARP, and computes how traffic should be forwarded.
Where the switch processes the protocols that manage the network. BPDUs are control-plane traffic, not user data.
Where the router runs its routing protocols, builds the RIB and decides where traffic should go.
Where Hellos, LSAs and SPF run. OSPF is control-plane work entirely — BPDUs and LSAs are not user traffic.
Where EIGRP’s hellos, updates, queries and DUAL run. Route selection is control-plane work; packet forwarding is not.
Where BGP sessions, best-path selection and policy run. Deciding which path to advertise is control-plane work.
Where redistribution decisions and policy are applied.
The plane that runs routing protocols and processes traffic addressed to the device.
The routing and signalling side: IGP, LDP, MP-BGP and the label and route exchanges that build the forwarding state.
The routing and signalling side of the device. QoS protects control traffic such as routing updates with CS6.
Control Plane Policing. Rate-limits traffic destined to the device CPU using ACLs, class-maps, policy-maps and policing.
The forwarding path for user packets; runs on ASICs/TCAM and is measured in pps and FIB entries.
The fast path where traffic is actually forwarded. Throughput, latency and per-packet actions such as ACL and QoS happen here.
Where packets are actually forwarded, using the FIB and adjacency tables through CEF.
Where packets are actually forwarded, using what SPF installed. A healthy LSDB does not by itself mean traffic flows.
Where packets are actually forwarded, typically by CEF from the FIB. EIGRP selects routes and never touches a packet itself.
Where packets are forwarded once BGP has chosen. A route can sit in the BGP table and still never forward because the next hop is unreachable.
Where traffic actually flows once routes are installed.
The plane that forwards transit traffic through the device.
The forwarding side, where CEF pushes labels and LSRs swap them through the LFIB.
The packet-forwarding side, where marking, queuing and dropping actually happen under a QoS policy.
The receiving side of encapsulation: bottom-up, each layer strips and validates its own header and trailer, then hands the payload to the layer above.
0.0.0.0/0 — the catch-all route consulted when nothing more specific matches. Longest-prefix match makes it the last route tried.
The catch-all route consulted when nothing more specific matches. In IPv6 it is learned from the Router Advertisement.
0.0.0.0/0, the least-specific catch-all. Used only when nothing more specific matches. A host calls it a default gateway.
The catch-all a stub, totally stubby or NSSA area relies on once external and inter-area specifics are filtered out.
The catch-all destination. In an EIGRP stub design it is often the only route an edge needs toward the hub.
The catch-all prefix. In PBR, set default next-hop is a fallback rather than an override, which is the distinction the exam tests.
A catch-all prefix sometimes redistributed to provide reachability from a stub domain.
The gateway hosts use; FHRPs make that gateway highly available.
The time a packet takes to travel a path, made up of serialization, propagation, processing and queueing components.
The practice of removing unnecessary services, disabling unused ports and applying control-plane protection to a network device.
Reducing the attack surface by disabling what is not needed and protecting what must remain. BPDU Guard on edge ports is part of it.
Reducing the attack surface of a device: strong secrets, SSH-only access, login rate limits, ACLs and disabled services.

Device hardening is the practice of locking down the device itself: disable unneeded services, enforce strong AAA, encrypt management, secure access lines, control-plane protection, and restrict remote config so the router/switch is not the soft target. It's the "defense at the box" layer...
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol — the automatic lease of an address, mask, gateway and DNS server to a host on a segment.
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol, which leases an address and options such as the gateway and DNS server to a client.
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol. UDP 67 server and UDP 68 client, DORA exchange, leases with T1 at 50% and T2 at 87.5%.
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol. It supplies client IP addresses, and mobility must preserve the address across a roam where possible.
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol. It supplies addresses on broadband, cellular and Ethernet links where address negotiation is not done by IPCP.

DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) automatically assigns IP parameters — address, mask, gateway, DNS, lease time — to hosts on boot. It replaces manual static configuration and is a core enterprise service: DORA, relays, snooping, and DHCPv6 all hang off it.
A router that forwards client DHCP requests across subnets to a central server, using the giaddr field so the reply reaches the right client.
Forwards DHCP between subnets using ip helper-address and fills giaddr so the server picks the right scope.
A switch security feature that builds a trust boundary around DHCP, so only trusted ports may send server replies, and which feeds the binding database used by DAI.
A Layer 2 control that marks the uplink toward the DHCP server as trusted, so rogue DHCP servers on untrusted ports are ignored.
Layer 2 switch security feature that blocks DHCP server messages on untrusted ports and builds a binding database.
Layer 2 feature that builds the IP to MAC binding table used by DAI and IP Source Guard.
The stateful IPv6 configuration protocol, with a multicast Solicit to ff02::1:2, client port 546 and server port 547.
Differentiated Services. A scalable per-class model where DSCP selects a per-hop behaviour, with no signalling or reservations.
AWS private connectivity from an enterprise location or colocation facility to AWS, bypassing the public Internet.
Dynamic Multipoint VPN. mGRE plus NHRP plus IPsec, giving a hub-and-spoke design with direct spoke-to-spoke tunnels.

DMVPN (Dynamic Multipoint VPN) is Cisco's hub-and-spoke site-to-site VPN that scales to hundreds/thousands of branches and builds dynamic spoke-to-spoke tunnels on demand: branches that need to talk directly bypass the hub (no hub bottleneck, no full-mesh config). Built on mGRE + NHRP + IPsec —...
Demilitarized Zone — the segmented zone between the untrusted Internet and the internal network.

Cisco Catalyst Center (formerly DNA Center) is the SDN controller + management platform for the campus: the heart of intent-based networking (IBN). It automates design, provisioning, assurance (telemetry/AI), and policy across switches/APs, and orchestrates SD-Access fabrics (VXLAN/LISP/ISE). It is the campus analog of...
Domain Name System. Resolves names to addresses over UDP 53 and TCP 53, with A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, PTR, NS, SRV and SOA records.

DNS (Domain Name System) maps names ↔ IP addresses (A/AAAA records), and much more (MX, CNAME, PTR). It's a hierarchical, distributed database: root → TLD → authoritative servers, with resolvers caching answers. UDP 53 (TCP 53 for large transfers/zone transfers).
Synthesizes AAAA records from A records to help IPv6 clients reach IPv4-only destinations.

Docker is the most common container runtime/platform: you write a Dockerfile (build recipe) → build an image (immutable snapshot) → share it via a registry (Docker Hub) → run containers anywhere Docker exists. It popularized containers with an easy CLI and tooling (Compose for multi-container...
Designated and Backup Designated Router, elected on broadcast and NBMA segments so each router adjacencies with only two others. Highest priority, then highest RID, non-preemptive.
Designated Router and Backup Designated Router concepts. In PIM the DR election uses priority and IP; the backup concept comes from OSPF.
The 6-bit Differentiated Services Code Point in the IP header, the Layer 3 marking used for QoS classification.
Differentiated Services Code Point. The 6-bit Layer 3 field that selects a per-hop behaviour, with values such as EF 46 and AF41 34.
Dynamic Trunking Protocol, a Cisco-proprietary protocol that negotiates whether a link becomes a trunk. It does not negotiate VLANs.
Dynamic Trunking Protocol — Cisco’s trunk negotiation. An access port that trunk-negotiates can bring DTP frames into the tree.
Diffusing Update Algorithm — EIGRP’s loop-free path selection. A neighbour’s reported distance must be strictly less than your feasible distance for the path to qualify as a backup.
Whether a link transmits and receives simultaneously (full duplex) or one direction at a time (half duplex).
Whether a link transmits and receives at the same time (full duplex) or one direction at a time (half duplex).
Whether a link transmits and receives simultaneously (full duplex) or one direction at a time (half duplex). Modern Ethernet is full duplex on dedicated switch ports.
A per-port control that validates ARP replies against the DHCP snooping binding database, blocking address spoofing.
Validates ARP packets against the DHCP snooping binding table to stop ARP spoofing.
Validates ARP packets on untrusted ports against DHCP snooping bindings or ARP ACLs to stop ARP spoofing.
Temporary one-to-one mappings from a NAT pool, typically for inside-initiated traffic.
Protocols that exchange reachability, build a topology view and converge automatically: distance vector, advanced distance vector, link state and path vector.
A BGP session between routers in different autonomous systems, carrying routes across the administrative boundary between them.
External BGP, between different autonomous systems. AD 20, TTL 1 by default, and the next hop is rewritten to the advertising router on every advertisement.
eBGP (External BGP) peer sessions run between routers in different autonomous systems. It is how one AS advertises its prefixes to the Internet and how the Internet exchanges routes at large.
Embedded Event Manager. An on-box automation feature that watches for an event, optionally tests a condition, and runs actions such as CLI commands, syslog, SNMP or email.
A Cisco-proprietary advanced distance-vector IGP combining distance-vector simplicity with fast convergence through the DUAL algorithm.
Cisco’s advanced distance vector protocol using DUAL, with a composite metric of bandwidth and delay by default, AD 90 internal and 170 external.
Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol — Cisco’s advanced distance-vector IGP, kept loop-free by DUAL and carried by RTP over IP protocol 88. Route code D, AD 90 internal and 170 external.
Hybrid distance-vector; redistributed routes become external (AD 170) and require a seed metric unless coming from certain protocols.
A Cisco advanced distance-vector IGP that can also serve as the PE to CE routing protocol in a VRF.

EIGRP (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol) is a Cisco-proprietary, advanced distance-vector (hybrid) IGP that combines distance-vector simplicity with link-state-like fast convergence, thanks to the DUAL algorithm and a reliable transport (RTP).
HMAC-MD5 in classic mode and HMAC-SHA-256 in named mode, configured per interface from a key chain. Not enabled by default, and it is not encryption.
EIGRP running over IPv6 with the same DUAL algorithm, composite metric and timers as IPv4 — only the addressing and configuration scaffolding differ.
The same DUAL and RTP engine over IPv6. Enabled per interface with no network command, multicast FF02::A, and next hops that are normally link-local.
The composite metric. By default only bandwidth and delay are used — K1 and K3 are 1 — with bandwidth the minimum along the path and delay cumulative.
The composite metric (bandwidth, delay, reliability, load, MTU). Used when redistributing into EIGRP as the seed metric.
A router that advertises a restricted route set and never forwards queries past itself. The default is connected plus summary, and it still learns normally.
Adding headers (and trailers) as data descends the layers, and removing them as it ascends at the receiver.
Adding headers and trailers as data travels down the protocol stack: application to transport to network to link. Each layer wraps the previous output in its own envelope.
Adding headers and trailers as data travels down the protocol stack: application to transport to network to link.
The way a protocol wraps its data for transmission, such as the 802.1Q encapsulation that binds a router subinterface to a VLAN.
A host that originates or consumes traffic — PC, phone, printer, server, IoT.
Host-based protection such as antivirus, EDR, host firewall and posture assessment. It complements network security rather than replacing it.
The complete site architecture — access, distribution and core plus the server, WAN, security and management modules.

The enterprise campus is the full in-building / between-buildings network serving users — plus its server, WAN, and security modules. It is not a single topology: it is the complete site architecture assembled from many patterns.
The structured organization of devices into functional modules: core, distribution, access, plus DC, WAN, and DMZ blocks.
Organising devices into functional modules — campus, WAN, data centre, branch — around the core, distribution and access hierarchy.

ERSPAN (Encapsulated Remote SPAN) mirrors traffic across a routed/IP network: mirrored packets are encapsulated in IP + GRE and sent to a destination on any reachable router/switch — analyzer can be anywhere, unlike local SPAN (same box). The GRE-encapsulated copies ride normal routing; the...
Bundling several links into one logical port (LACP) for bandwidth and redundancy.
Bundling parallel physical links into one logical link for more bandwidth and link-level redundancy. The bundle counts as a single STP port.
An aggregate of several physical links presented as one logical interface. The bundle is then configured as an access port or a trunk.
Bundles parallel physical links into one logical link so STP sees a single port and the topology carries more aggregate bandwidth.

EtherChannel bundles parallel physical links into one logical link — more bandwidth, link-level redundancy, and loop-free simplicity (the bundle is ONE STP port). Negotiation: LACP (IEEE 802.3ad, standard) or PAgP (Cisco); static channels also exist. All links must match (speed/duplex/VLANs) and...
The dominant LAN standard (IEEE 802.3): a family of frame formats, signalling, speeds and media from 10 Mbps hubs to 400 Gbps fabrics.
IEEE 802.3, the dominant LAN standard: a family of frame formats, signalling, speeds and media from shared 10 Mbps hubs to 400 Gbps fabrics.
The Layer 2 LAN technology used as the physical and service foundation for PPPoE, Metro Ethernet and most WAN edge links.
The Layer 2 PDU that carries IPv4, IPv6 and ARP across Ethernet. Addressing, EtherType, payload and a 4-byte FCS make up the de facto Ethernet II format.
The Layer 2 unit of Ethernet, with destination and source MAC addresses, a type field, payload and frame check sequence.
The 802.3 sub-amendments whose names encode speed–signalling–medium, so decoding one tells you the cable, optics and reach.
The EEM component that watches for a trigger such as a syslog message, SNMP object, timer, interface change or tracking state.
Azure private connectivity through a provider or colocation facility, designed for predictable latency and bandwidth.
The rule RD strictly less than FD. RD equal to FD does not qualify, and neither does a greater RD — that strictness is what guarantees loop freedom.
A backup path that passes the feasibility condition and is therefore proven loop-free. Held in the topology table, promoted with no queries when the successor fails.
Forwarding Equivalence Class. A set of packets that share the same forwarding treatment and therefore one label.
The Forwarding Information Base — the forwarding-optimised copy of the routing table built by CEF, with next hops already resolved into Layer 2 rewrites.
Forwarding Information Base — the data-plane lookup structure derived from the RIB, worked on with the adjacency table.
Forwarding Information Base. The forwarding copy of the routing table, held per VRF when VRFs are used.

The FIB (Forwarding Information Base) is the data-plane, forwarding-optimized copy of the routing table — built by CEF from the RIB with next hops already resolved into L2 rewrites. Packets are switched against the FIB, not against the RIB: longest-prefix FIB lookup → adjacency rewrite →...
Cable carrying light through a glass core by total internal reflection: longer reach, higher bandwidth and total EMI immunity.
Deliberately not sending a frame out a given port. The classic case is a frame whose destination was learned on the same ingress port.
HSRP or VRRP — lets two routers share one virtual default gateway so a failure is not a blackout.
A protocol that gives hosts a single virtual default gateway backed by several routers, so a standby takes over the same virtual IP and MAC.
A protocol providing a redundant default gateway for hosts using a shared virtual IP and virtual MAC.

An FHRP (First Hop Redundancy Protocol) gives end hosts a single virtual default gateway backed by multiple real routers — if the active router dies, a standby takes over the same virtual IP and MAC, so hosts keep working without any client reconfiguration. FHRPs are the "make the default...

Flexible NetFlow (FNF) is the configurable NetFlow engine: you define the records — match = the flow key fields, collect = the extra fields to gather (which switches/extended features first made this usable). Built from three pieces: record → exporter → monitor (bound to an interface). It's also...
Cisco IKEv2-based VPN framework built from proposal, policy, keyring and profile blocks, covering site-to-site and remote access.
A static route with an AD higher than the primary source, so it installs only when that route is gone. Below 255, which means unreachable.
Sending a frame out every port in the same VLAN except the ingress port, when the destination MAC is unknown, the frame is a broadcast, or a multicast is being flooded.
Sending a frame out every port except the one it arrived on. Loops turn flooding into a broadcast storm.
Fixed Length Subnet Masking — every subnet gets the same prefix length. Simple and predictable, wasteful when requirements vary.
Choosing the egress port for a received frame from the destination MAC plus VLAN lookup in the MAC address table.
File Transfer Protocol. TCP 21 control and separate data connection, TCP 20 in active mode, cleartext credentials.
Group Encrypted Transport VPN. Tunnel-free any-to-any encryption using a GDOI group key distributed by a Key Server on UDP 848.

Git is a distributed version control system (Linus Torvalds, 2005): it tracks changes to files — configs, scripts, playbooks — with commits, branches, and rollback. For network engineers: the backbone of "config as code", enabling review, history, and instant revert of device configurations and...
Cisco FHRP providing redundancy and load balancing using AVG and up to four AVFs, UDP 3222, multicast 224.0.0.102.
IPv6 public unicast space, 2000::/3 — the Internet-routable addresses, normally obtained from a provider prefix by SLAAC or DHCPv6.
gRPC Network Management Interface. An open model-driven interface that streams YANG-encoded state and supports configuration operations over gRPC.
Unsolicited ARP announcing "my IP is at my MAC". Used for duplicate-address detection, MAC change notification and fast first-hop failover.
Generic Routing Encapsulation. IP protocol 47 tunnel that carries any L3 payload, including multicast, with no encryption of its own.

High Availability is the discipline of layering redundancy at every level — power, link (EtherChannel), device (Redundant Supervisors, stacking), gateway (FHRP), path (routing) — to reach a business availability target (e.g. 99.999% / five nines ≈ 5 min/year down). Good HA design matches...
Cisco FHRP using Active/Standby, UDP 1985, multicast 224.0.0.2 (v1) or 224.0.0.102 (v2).

HSRP (Hot Standby Router Protocol) is Cisco's proprietary FHRP: two or more routers share a virtual IP + virtual MAC; one is Active, the others Standby. If Active dies, Standby takes over in seconds (hello 3 s, hold 10 s; subsecond with timers). Virtual MAC: 0000.0c07.acXX (XX = group).
Stateless web request and response protocol on TCP 80, using methods such as GET and POST.
HTTP over TLS on TCP 443, authenticating the server with a certificate.

A hybrid cloud combines on-premises and public cloud into one operating model: shared networking, security, and management between both, so workloads can burst (overflow to public), backup, or replicate across the boundary. The network is the glue: VPN/IPsec, Direct Connect/ExpressRoute, SD-WAN...
A combination of two or more base topologies in one network. Real deployments are almost always hybrids.

A hypervisor (VMM) is the software that creates and runs VMs by abstracting hardware and multiplexing it between guests. Type 1 (bare-metal) runs directly on hardware — the datacenter standard (ESXi, KVM, Hyper-V, Xen). Type 2 (hosted) runs as an app on an OS (VirtualBox, VMware Workstation) —...

IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) delivers raw compute, storage, and networking on demand: you rent VMs (vCPU/vRAM), disks, and virtual networks (VPC) and manage everything above — OS, apps, data (AWS EC2, Azure VM, GCP Compute). The provider handles the physical/hypervisor layer. More control...
A BGP session between routers inside the same autonomous system, normally over loopback addresses and subject to the split-horizon rules.
Internal BGP, inside one autonomous system. AD 200, the next hop is preserved so the edge needs next-hop-self, and split horizon forces a full mesh or reflectors.
iBGP (Internal BGP) peer sessions run between routers in the same AS. Its job is to carry the BGP routes from border to border without redistributing them into the IGP.
IPv6 control protocol number 58, carrying error reporting, echo, neighbour discovery and MLD. It is required for IPv6 to function.
Internet Group Management Protocol — the host-to-router membership protocol that tells the local router which multicast groups a receiver wants to join.
Internet Group Management Protocol. Host-to-router membership signalling on a LAN, with v3 adding source filtering.
The switch feature that listens to IGMP joins and leaves and builds a Layer 2 multicast forwarding table, so multicast stops behaving like a flood.
Switch feature that inspects IGMP reports and forwards multicast only to member ports plus the mrouter port.
Internet Key Exchange version 2, RFC 7296. Modern IPsec key management with IKE_SA_INIT and IKE_AUTH, native NAT-T and EAP.

IKEv2 (Internet Key Exchange version 2) is the modern IPsec key-management protocol — it establishes and maintains the security associations (SAs) and session keys used to encrypt traffic. It replaced IKEv1's two-phase complexity with a leaner exchange, built-in mobility, NAT traversal, and EAP...
Internet Message Access Protocol. TCP 143 or 993 secure, keeps mail on the server and synchronises across devices.
Public IP address representing an inside host as seen from the outside network.
Private IP address of an inside host as seen from the inside network.
Forwarding traffic between the Layer 3 subnets of different VLANs, using router subinterfaces, switch SVIs or routed access ports.
Moving traffic between VLANs, which requires a Layer 3 boundary. Trunks carry the VLANs to it.
A device that forwards, filters, or secures traffic between end devices: switch, router, firewall, AP.
Integrated Services. A per-flow model that reserves resources with RSVP for hard guarantees and does not scale well.
